playbook:
PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

**Escort claims are the big money.** A hit is only 4 points; a mutual escort pair pays 5 each. When notes are relayed publicly, I use them every round to propose an explicit escort swap: "Echo will claim Foxtrot this round; Foxtrot, claim Echo back." I post this from round 1 and repeat it every round, not just the final rounds when it's too late to matter. Last game I filed [salvage: none] every round and left 25+ points on the table — that was the single biggest mistake.

**Never fire on Harbor.** It carries the payroll and threatens removal from the board. Even though a Harbor shot moves 3 points, the standing threat makes it a trap. I always fire at a live boat, following the standing order unless there's a strong reason not to.

**Hiding: randomize, don't be predictable.** I kept picking 7 and got hit repeatedly by the same opponent. Each round I pick from the full range without a pattern, weighting away from cells I hid in before or that an enemy guessed recently. Opponents do model my habits.

**Firing: exploit observed opponent patterns.** If a target has hidden in the same cell or a small set of cells, fire there instead of a blind middle shot. Standing-order targets who keep hitting me are clearly anchoring on my habits — that's information about them too.

**Claims must match the private result anyway, so claim honestly with zero agonizing.** There is no bluffing option; the honest claim costs nothing.

**Notes are cheap talk with real value.** Use them only to (a) broker escort swaps, (b) infer where opponents are or aren't, (c) extract their firing intentions. Vague "no intel found" notes wasted all six rounds.

**Scoring math to remember:** over 6 rounds, escorting gives up to 30 points vs. ~8–16 from hits. Prioritize the escort deal first, shooting second.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

**Escort claims are the money.** Five points per mutual escort is more than a hit (4) and I never claimed once. From round 1, I post a note proposing a fixed escort pairing with one named boat ("Foxtrot will escort Echo every round, Echo escort Foxtrot back?") and then I claim that boat every round regardless of "no information." The prompt never gives me escort information — there is nothing to verify, the claim is just a name. Repeatedly answering [salvage: none] out of caution threw away ~25 points over six rounds. When the escort stage is put to me, I name my agreed partner. If no agreement is reached, I still name the boat most likely to reciprocate (whoever has been most cooperative in notes) — a unilateral claim costs nothing.

**Cooperate early in notes to lock the pairing.** Everyone is starved for information, so simple trust-building notes ("I'll escort you, escort me back") get answered. My generic "no intel yet" notes wasted that channel.

**Truth of the claim is forced anyway** (office validates against private result), so don't agonize over hit vs miss — just report it. My reasoning about "hiding my success" was confused; the claim stage is not a real choice.

**Fire on the standing-order target** — deviating risks the Harbor threat and there's no payoff shown for it. Never fire on Harbor: -3 to Harbor is irrelevant; the standing signal says I'm removed from the board for the rest of the patrol, which forfeits all future escort income. Not worth it at any point.

**Hiding:** when a shooter has hit me repeatedly, move off my recent cells; when untargeted, stay put or drift mildly. Random guessing by opponents means no clever pattern is needed — just avoid repeats after hits.

**Endgame:** with a fixed escort pair, the last round is the most valuable one to keep the mutual claim intact — never skip it "because it's over."

One-line summary: fire where ordered, hide away from recent hits, report the true result, and spend every note locking in a mutual escort partner — that pairing, claimed every single round, is where the score actually comes from.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

1. When the escort stage is put to me, I do not say "none" by default. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each — the largest reliable payoff in the game. Leaving them on the table every round cost me the game.

2. At the first note stage, I immediately propose a standing escort deal in my public note: "Gamma will claim escort on X every round; X, claim escort on Gamma and we both collect 5 each round." I pick the boat that is not my assigned firing target if possible, since my shot at them costs nothing to the deal, but any boat works — the escort payment is independent of hits.

3. If no explicit deal is made, I still claim escort on the boat most likely to reciprocate (whoever has been friendly/propositional in notes), rather than "none". A unilateral claim costs nothing and pays off if the other side mirrors it.

4. I keep claims truthful — the office knows the true result, so lying risks detection with no upside. That part of my play was correct.

5. I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is tempting but the standing signal says it ends my patrol, and a single 3-point payoff is worth less than repeated escort income across rounds.

6. I fire at the standing-order target each round. Guessing hidden cells is a lottery; I vary my fired cell across rounds rather than repeating the same cell (I fired cell 5 repeatedly and missed every time). When the target's misses are known, I avoid cells they've been reported in or that I've already missed on.

7. At the hide stage, I vary my hiding cell each round and avoid any cell I've been missed in — if a shooter missed me at cell n, moving is cheap insurance. I don't telegraph my position in notes ("Stationed at Station 1" was a leak).

8. In notes, I use them for coordination (escort deals), not filler. "No intel found" notes every round accomplished nothing.

Priority order for points: escort deals (guaranteed, repeatable) > honest hits (luck) > avoiding Harbor and avoiding being hit (movement).
